query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled heat treatment of a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a metastable, homogeneous solid‐solution state initiates diffusion‐driven nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. When the treatment is moderate, these precipitates remain fine and help maintain the integrity of the protective oxide film, thereby retaining corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance; when the treatment is too aggressive, the precipitates coarsen and form continuous networks that disrupt the oxide scale and degrade environmental resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy produced under nonequilibrium conditions, with a homogeneous, metastable solid-solution microstructure and a uniformly protective oxide film.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled heat treatment/thermal aging protocol.
generation.conditions: A controlled comparison between as-cast (metastable) samples and samples aged under defined thermal regimes; with moderate aging (e.g., lower temperature and/or shorter duration) versus more aggressive aging (e.g., higher temperature and/or longer duration) delineating the service-regime boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, size, and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates (initially nanoscale under moderate conditions and coarsened under aggressive conditions).
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation enhances atomic diffusion in the metastable state, triggering a diffusion-controlled transformation. Under moderate conditions, fine, dispersed Mg-rich intermetallics form that locally alter chemistry in a way that reinforces the protective oxide film; if the thermal exposure exceeds a critical threshold, the intermetallic phases coarsen into networks that disrupt oxide continuity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial state, samples aged under moderate conditions will exhibit a microstructure with finely dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates and stable corrosion/high-temperature oxidation resistance, whereas samples aged under more aggressive conditions will show coarsened intermetallic networks accompanied by a measurable deterioration in oxide integrity and environmental resistance.
generation.baseline: The as-cast metastable solid-solution state with uniform phase distribution and established corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: Service regimes demarcated by thermal treatment conditions (temperature and time) that separate the moderate aging regime where fine precipitates are maintained from the aggressive regime where precipitate coarsening occurs.
generation.uncertainty: The critical temperature/time thresholds for the transformation may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing history; further experiments are needed to define these boundaries precisely.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to moderate heat treatment (e.g., at a lower temperature and/or for a shorter duration) and the other set to aggressive heat treatment (e.g., at a higher temperature or for a longer duration). Use the as-cast metastable state as the control. After treatment, characterize the microstructure via electron microscopy (TEM/SEM) and phase analysis (XRD). Additionally, perform standardized corrosion tests (such as potentiodynamic polarization in NaCl solution) and high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., weight gain measurements) to assess oxide film quality.
measurements: Microstructural imaging and precipitate size/distribution analysis (TEM/SEM)
Phase identification via XRD
Oxide scale integrity assessment (e.g., XPS, impedance spectroscopy)
Corrosion rate measurements (potentiodynamic polarization)
High-temperature oxidation kinetics (e.g., weight gain measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If moderate heat treatment does not result in the formation of fine, dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates or if both the moderate and aggressive heat-treated samples exhibit similar microstructures and identical corrosion/oxidation performance relative to the as-cast state, then the hypothesis—that controlled diffusion-mediated precipitation governs the retention versus loss of environmental resistance—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Magnesium-containing multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are promising for lightweight applications due to their low density, high specific strength, and biocompatibility. This study examines two Mg-Ti-Zn alloy compositions, equal molar MgTiZn (TZ) and Mg4TiZn (4TZ), synthesized via ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering, focusing on their microstructures and corrosion behaviors. X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy revealed the formation of intermetallic phases, including Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25 in TZ, while 4TZ exhibited a predominantly Mg-rich phase. Potentiodynamic polarization and immersion tests in 0.1 M NaCl solution showed that both alloys had good corrosion resistance, with values of 3.65 ± 0.65 µA/cm2 for TZ and 4.58 ± 1.64 µA/cm2 for 4TZ. This was attributed to the formation of a TiO2-rich surface film in the TZ, as confirmed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), which contributed to enhanced passivation and lower corrosion current density. drafts.hypothesis: Heat treatment (or prolonged service exposure) of a Mg-containing lightweight HEA in a metastable solid-solution state induces local decomposition via nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases. These intermetallic phases disturb the continuity of the protective oxide layer, thereby compromising corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, homogeneous metastable solid-solution state.
drafts.intervention: Controlled heat treatment at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–800°C) for extended durations or simulated service exposure within this temperature range.
drafts.conditions: A controlled comparison between as-cast/metastable samples and samples subjected to the specified heat treatment/service conditions, with the key variable being the thermal history that governs phase instability.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
drafts.mechanism: The formation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases disrupts the uniformity and integrity of the initially protective oxide layer. This structural change creates preferential sites for corrosion and oxidation, thus explaining the transformed performance of the alloy.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial state, heat-treated samples will exhibit a transformed microstructure characterized by discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. This will correlate with a reduction or loss in uniform protective oxide formation and a measurable decline in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast alloy with a homogeneous, metastable solid-solution microstructure and an intact, uniformly protective oxide film.
drafts.boundary: Service regimes where temperature exceeds approximately 600°C for prolonged periods, under which significant intermetallic phase formation and consequent microstructural degradation are expected. Lower thermal exposures may not trigger the same level of transformation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy specimens: one retained in the as-cast (metastable) state and another subjected to controlled heat treatment at 700°C for a series of time intervals. Use high-resolution electron microscopy (e.g., SEM/EDS, TEM) and XRD to characterize the emergence and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic phases. Concurrently, perform standardized corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation tests to assess the protective film behavior.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification via XRD and microscopy (SEM/EDS, TEM)
Distribution mapping of Mg-rich intermetallics
Corrosion rate measurements (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization tests)
Oxidation weight gain measurements during high-temperature exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a significant increase in Mg-rich intermetallic phase formation compared to the as-cast state, or if there is no corresponding measurable degradation in corrosion and oxidation resistance, then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state, controlled thermal aging within a moderate temperature regime triggers spinodal-like decomposition that selectively precipitates nanoscale, Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. These fine precipitates form primarily along grain boundaries and within the matrix, locally altering the chemistry to promote the formation of a stable, protective oxide layer. However, if aging conditions (temperature and time) exceed a critical threshold, these intermetallic precipitates coarsen into continuous networks that disrupt oxide layer integrity, resulting in a marked loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state with high Mg supersaturation in a disordered high-entropy alloy matrix.
drafts.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal aging treatment with two regimes: one at a moderate temperature to promote slow, fine-scale precipitation, and a second at a higher temperature or prolonged duration to drive rapid coarsening of precipitates.
drafts.conditions: Service-regime boundaries are defined by moderate temperature/time conditions (e.g., approximately 300–500°C for controlled aging) versus higher temperature or extended aging conditions that lead to accelerated intermetallic growth.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that initially appear as nanoscale features and then coarsen under more aggressive aging conditions.
drafts.mechanism: Thermal activation causes spinodal-like decomposition in the metastable matrix, leading to the nucleation and growth of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates initially act as barriers to rapid diffusion, promoting a stable, passivating oxide scale. If the aging exceeds a critical kinetic threshold, the precipitates coarsen into continuous phase networks that compromise the integrity of the oxide layer and yield increased susceptibility to corrosion and oxidation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under moderate aging conditions, the alloy will exhibit a fine, dispersed precipitate microstructure with retained corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance compared to the initial state. Under more aggressive aging conditions, coarsening of intermetallic compounds will be observed, accompanied by a significant reduction in protective oxide quality and thus lower resistance to corrosion and oxidation.
drafts.baseline: The initial non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state with homogeneous distribution and baseline resistance properties before any significant thermal aging.
drafts.boundary: The critical boundaries are the thermal treatment conditions – specifically, temperatures around 300–500°C and corresponding time durations – below which fine precipitate formation is maintained and above which coarsening leads to deterioration of protective properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the Mg-containing high-entropy alloy and subject them to two controlled thermal aging treatments: one in the moderate regime (e.g., 300–500°C for a specified time) and one in a higher regime (e.g., >500°C or significantly longer durations). Use identical initial processing to ensure baseline uniformity. Characterize the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess precipitate size, distribution, and phase evolution, and correlate these findings with corrosion and high-temperature oxidation tests.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (TEM, SEM) to quantify precipitate size and distribution
Phase identification via XRD to detect intermetallic formation
Surface characterization of oxide scale integrity (e.g., XPS, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
Corrosion rate measurements in simulated service environments
High-temperature oxidation weight gain measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging under moderate conditions does not result in the formation of nanoscale precipitates or if both aging regimes show similar microstructures and identical corrosion/oxidation performance, then the hypothesis that controlled precipitation governs the retention versus loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys that initially exist as a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution, thermally activated diffusion leads to the nucleation and growth of intermetallic precipitates—especially along grain boundaries—that locally deplete or enrich oxide‐forming elements. This microstructural evolution modulates the formation and integrity of protective oxide films during high-temperature exposure and alters the alloy’s corrosion behavior.
drafts.material_initial_state: A metastable, homogeneous solid solution in a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy produced via rapid solidification or similar nonequilibrium processing.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to isothermal heat treatments at service-relevant temperatures (e.g., 800–950 °C) for controlled durations.
drafts.conditions: A controlled comparison between as-cast (metastable) samples and samples aged under defined thermal conditions; subsequent evaluation under high-temperature oxidation (in air) and corrosion tests (e.g., in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution).
drafts.structural_mediator: The development of intermetallic coarse precipitates—preferentially nucleating at or near grain boundaries—that alter local elemental distributions.
drafts.mechanism: Thermal activation enhances element diffusion, triggering the segregation and clustering of reactive species that form intermetallic compounds. This process changes the local chemistry, influencing the ability of key elements (e.g., Mg and accompanying species such as Ti) to form a uniform, protective oxide layer during high temperature exposure and, concurrently, affecting galvanic interactions during corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will show a microstructure with observable intermetallic precipitates and grain boundary segregation. Depending on the morphology and distribution of these phases, the alloy may exhibit either improved oxidation resistance (if a coherent, passivating oxide forms) or degraded performance (if precipitate-induced chemical inhomogeneity promotes localized corrosion). The as-cast samples, by contrast, will retain their original homogeneous corrosion and oxidation behavior.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast metastable solid solution state with a uniform phase distribution and established baseline levels of corrosion current density and oxidation weight gain.
drafts.boundary: Service regimes characterized by elevated temperatures (approximately 800–950 °C) and corrosive environments (e.g., exposure to 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) where diffusion kinetics and phase transformations become significant.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples from the same Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy. Subject one group to isothermal heat treatments at 900 °C for incrementally increasing durations while keeping the other group in its as-cast state. After treatment, characterize the microstructure using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron microscopy to quantify intermetallic precipitation and grain boundary segregation. Subsequently, perform corrosion testing (potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt.% NaCl) and high-temperature oxidation studies (measuring weight gain in air).
measurements: Phase identification and quantification (via XRD and TEM/SEM)
Grain boundary/intermetallic precipitate distribution
Corrosion current density and pitting potential
Oxidation weight gain/trend over time at elevated temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show significant intermetallic formation or chemical segregation relative to the as-cast state, and if their corrosion and oxidation resistance do not change measurably, the proposed mechanism—that diffusion-driven precipitation governs the evolution of environmental resistance—would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Prolonged exposure of the metastable, homogeneous Mg‐containing high-entropy alloy to service‐relevant temperatures (800–1000 °C) initiates a diffusion‐controlled transformation that nucleates and grows fine intermetallic precipitates (primarily along grain boundaries). These precipitates, by consuming or redistributing key passivating elements, modify the chemistry at the alloy/oxide interface and thereby alter the continuity and protective nature of the oxide scale. As a result, the alloy’s high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion behavior will either be retained (if a continuous, protective oxide is promoted) or degraded (if nonuniform intermetallic coarsening leads to discontinuous oxide formation).
drafts.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a non-equilibrium, homogeneous solid-solution state
drafts.intervention: Thermal aging at service temperatures (e.g., 800–1000 °C) for an extended duration
drafts.conditions: Exposures performed in an oxidizing environment (air) and compared with a controlled sample maintained at lower temperatures (non-aged state)
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates forming preferentially along grain boundaries
drafts.mechanism: Thermal exposure enhances diffusion, leading to elemental segregation and nucleation of intermetallic compounds. This transformation alters the local chemistry at grain boundaries, either promoting a passivating oxide (by concentrating oxide-forming elements like Ti) or interrupting oxide continuity if precipitate coarsening is nonuniform.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous state, thermally aged samples will exhibit distinct intermetallic phases detectable by XRD and TEM, with corresponding changes in oxide scale morphology on the surface. Electrochemical tests and high-temperature oxidation measurements will show either improved or diminished corrosion/oxidation resistance, depending on the uniformity and nature of the precipitate-induced modification of the protective scale.
drafts.baseline: The initial metastable solid solution, with its homogeneous distribution of alloying elements, develops a continuous, protective oxide layer that accounts for its high corrosion and oxidation resistance.
drafts.boundary: Service regimes at temperatures between 800 and 1000 °C over durations sufficient for diffusion (e.g., >100 hours), beyond which the kinetics of intermetallic nucleation and growth become significant.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing HEA samples. Subject one set to extended thermal aging at a service-relevant temperature (e.g., 900 °C for 100 hours) in air, while keeping the other as a low-temperature (unaged) control. Characterize both groups using XRD and TEM to detect phase changes and intermetallic precipitate formation; conduct high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., weight gain measurements) and corrosion tests (e.g., electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) to evaluate changes in protective behavior.
measurements: XRD for phase identification and evolution
TEM for imaging precipitate morphology and distribution
High-temperature oxidation (weight gain) testing
Electrochemical corrosion measurements (potentiodynamic polarization, impedance spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not show significant formation of intermetallic precipitates or if the oxide scale morphology and corrosion/oxidation resistance remain statistically indistinguishable from the unaged control, then the hypothesis that the diffusion-controlled transformation of the metastable state into an intermetallic-containing microstructure governs the change in protective behavior is falsified.
